claim: A systematic screen for yeast mutants revealed that mutations in any of ~500 genes affects telomere length in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: A systematic screen for yeast mutants that affect telomere length maintenance in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae revealed that mutations in any of ~500 genes affects telomere length.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to systematic screens mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: ELG1 is one of the genes that, when mutated, causes telomere elongation.
source: One of the genes that, when mutated, causes telomere elongation is ELG1, which encodes an unloader of PCNA, the processivity factor for replicative DNA polymerases.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ELG1 encodes an unloader of PCNA, the processivity factor for replicative DNA polymerases.
source: One of the genes that, when mutated, causes telomere elongation is ELG1, which encodes an unloader of PCNA, the processivity factor for replicative DNA polymerases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Elg1 function, cited in the manuscript.

claim: PCNA can undergo SUMOylation on two conserved residues, K164 and K127.
source: PCNA can undergo SUMOylation on two conserved residues, K164 and K127, or ubiquitination at lysine 164.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCNA modifications.

claim: PCNA can undergo ubiquitination at lysine 164.
source: PCNA can undergo SUMOylation on two conserved residues, K164 and K127, or ubiquitination at lysine 164.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCNA modifications.

claim: SUMOylated PCNA acts as a signal that positively regulates telomerase activity.
source: We report that SUMOylated PCNA acts as a signal that positively regulates telomerase activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Physical interactions exist between Elg1 and the CST (Cdc13-Stn1-Ten) complex.
source: We also uncovered physical interactions between Elg1 and the CST (Cdc13-Stn1-Ten) complex and addressed the mechanism by which Elg1 and Stn1 negatively regulates telomere elongation, coordinated by SUMO.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Elg1 and Stn1 negatively regulate telomere elongation, coordinated by SUMO.
source: We also uncovered physical interactions between Elg1 and the CST (Cdc13-Stn1-Ten) complex and addressed the mechanism by which Elg1 and Stn1 negatively regulates telomere elongation, coordinated by SUMO.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genetic and biochemical data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Telomeric DNA consists of G/C-rich DNA repeats, with the G-rich strand extending to form a 3' single-stranded overhang.
source: Telomeric DNA consists of G/C-rich DNA repeats, with the G-rich strand extending to form a 3' single-stranded overhang.
evidence: This is established knowledge about telomere structure.

claim: Telomeres are primarily involved in counteracting the gradual shortening of the telomeric DNA caused by conventional DNA replication, thereby solving the 'end-replication problem'.
source: Telomeres are primarily involved in counteracting the gradual shortening of the telomeric DNA caused by conventional DNA replication, thereby solving the 'end-replication problem' (Bonnell et al., 2021; Soudet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Telomeres protect chromosome ends from improper recognition as a DNA double-strand break (DSB).
source: Another important function of telomeres is to protect chromosome ends from improper recognition as a DNA double-strand break (DSB) (reviewed in de Lange, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The CST complex in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is composed of Cdc13, Stn1, and Ten1.
source: An important, conserved protein complex involved in the regulation of telomere length is the CST, which in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is composed of Cdc13, Stn1, and Ten1 (Chen and Lingner, 2013; Ge et al., 2020; Lim et al., 2020; Puglisi et al., 2008; Rice and Skordalakes, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CST has similarity to the ssDNA binding complex RPA.
source: The CST has similarity to the ssDNA binding complex RPA and localizes specifically to the single-stranded telomeric DNA, where it is involved in chromosome end capping and telomere length regulation (Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Mersaoui and Wellinger, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CST localizes specifically to the single-stranded telomeric DNA.
source: The CST has similarity to the ssDNA binding complex RPA and localizes specifically to the single-stranded telomeric DNA, where it is involved in chromosome end capping and telomere length regulation (Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Mersaoui and Wellinger, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CST is involved in chromosome end capping and telomere length regulation.
source: The CST has similarity to the ssDNA binding complex RPA and localizes specifically to the single-stranded telomeric DNA, where it is involved in chromosome end capping and telomere length regulation (Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Mersaoui and Wellinger, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CST facilitates telomerase-mediated telomere elongation.
source: The CST facilitates telomerase-mediated telomere elongation (Evans and Lundblad, 1999; Evans and Lundblad, 2000; Nugent et al., 1996), participates in telomere processing during DNA replication (Soudet et al., 2014), and helps 'capping' the telomere (Mersaoui and Wellinger, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CST participates in telomere processing during DNA replication.
source: The CST facilitates telomerase-mediated telomere elongation (Evans and Lundblad, 1999; Evans and Lundblad, 2000; Nugent et al., 1996), participates in telomere processing during DNA replication (Soudet et al., 2014), and helps 'capping' the telomere (Mersaoui and Wellinger, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In late S-phase, Cdc13 interacts with the Est1 subunit of telomerase and promotes telomerase activity.
source: In late S-phase, Cdc13 interacts with the Est1 subunit of telomerase and promotes telomerase activity (Chandra et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stn1 binds Cdc13 in a region that overlaps with that bound by Est1.
source: Stn1 binds Cdc13 in a region that overlaps with that bound by Est1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CST complex interactions.

claim: Recruitment of Stn1 evicts Est1 and prevents further elongation of the G-strand.
source: Recruitment of Stn1 evicts Est1 and prevents further elongation of the G-strand (Chandra et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The amino terminus of Stn1 binds Ten1.
source: The amino terminus of Stn1 binds Ten1, whereas its C-terminus interacts with both Cdc13 and Pol12, a subunit of Polymerase Alpha (Grossi et al., 2004; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The C-terminus of Stn1 interacts with both Cdc13 and Pol12, a subunit of Polymerase Alpha.
source: The amino terminus of Stn1 binds Ten1, whereas its C-terminus interacts with both Cdc13 and Pol12, a subunit of Polymerase Alpha (Grossi et al., 2004; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CST coordinates leading strand elongation by telomerase with lagging strand DNA synthesis by the cell's replisome.
source: Thus, the CST coordinates leading strand elongation by telomerase with lagging strand DNA synthesis by the cell's replisome (Grossi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Loss of the ELG1 gene causes gross chromosomal rearrangements in S. cerevisiae.
source: In S. cerevisiae, loss of the ELG1 gene causes gross chromosomal rearrangements, chromosome losses, defective sister chromatid cohesion and recombination, increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, and abnormal telomere length maintenance (reviewed in Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Loss of the ELG1 gene causes chromosome losses in S. cerevisiae.
source: In S. cerevisiae, loss of the ELG1 gene causes gross chromosomal rearrangements, chromosome losses, defective sister chromatid cohesion and recombination, increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, and abnormal telomere length maintenance (reviewed in Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Loss of the ELG1 gene causes defective sister chromatid cohesion and recombination in S. cerevisiae.
source: In S. cerevisiae, loss of the ELG1 gene causes gross chromosomal rearrangements, chromosome losses, defective sister chromatid cohesion and recombination, increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, and abnormal telomere length maintenance (reviewed in Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Loss of the ELG1 gene causes increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents in S. cerevisiae.
source: In S. cerevisiae, loss of the ELG1 gene causes gross chromosomal rearrangements, chromosome losses, defective sister chromatid cohesion and recombination, increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, and abnormal telomere length maintenance (reviewed in Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Loss of the ELG1 gene causes abnormal telomere length maintenance in S. cerevisiae.
source: In S. cerevisiae, loss of the ELG1 gene causes gross chromosomal rearrangements, chromosome losses, defective sister chromatid cohesion and recombination, increased sensitivity to DNA damaging agents, and abnormal telomere length maintenance (reviewed in Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The function of the Elg1 RLC is to unload the processivity factor PCNA from chromatin.
source: The function of the Elg1 RLC is to unload the processivity factor PCNA from chromatin, in particular after Okazaki fragment processing and ligation in the lagging strand, and during DNA repair (Kubota et al., 2015; Kubota et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2010; Shemesh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The mammalian ortholog of ELG1 is ATAD5.
source: The mammalian ortholog of ELG1 (ATAD5) participates in the Fanconi Anemia pathway (Kim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2011) and, when mutated, leads to genome instability and cancer in mice and humans (Bell et al., 2011; Kuchenbaecker et al., 2015; Maleva Kostovska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ATAD5 participates in the Fanconi Anemia pathway.
source: The mammalian ortholog of ELG1 (ATAD5) participates in the Fanconi Anemia pathway (Kim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2011) and, when mutated, leads to genome instability and cancer in mice and humans (Bell et al., 2011; Kuchenbaecker et al., 2015; Maleva Kostovska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in ATAD5 lead to genome instability and cancer in mice and humans.
source: The mammalian ortholog of ELG1 (ATAD5) participates in the Fanconi Anemia pathway (Kim et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2011) and, when mutated, leads to genome instability and cancer in mice and humans (Bell et al., 2011; Kuchenbaecker et al., 2015; Maleva Kostovska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Elg1 RLC shows affinity to SUMOylated PCNA.
source: Although the Elg1 RLC shows affinity to SUMOylated PCNA, the complex is able to unload modified and unmodified versions of the clamp (Kang et al., 2019; Kubota et al., 2015; Kubota et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2010; Shemesh et al., 2017; Shiomi and Nishitani, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Elg1 RLC is able to unload modified and unmodified versions of PCNA.
source: Although the Elg1 RLC shows affinity to SUMOylated PCNA, the complex is able to unload modified and unmodified versions of the clamp (Kang et al., 2019; Kubota et al., 2015; Kubota et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2010; Shemesh et al., 2017; Shiomi and Nishitani, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SUMOylation may assist but is not essential for PCNA unloading.
source: Thus SUMOylation may assist but is not essential for PCNA unloading.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature.

claim: Retention and accumulation of PCNA on DNA is the major cause of genome instability in elg1Δ.
source: Retention and accumulation of PCNA on DNA is the major cause of genome instability in elg1Δ (Itzkovich et al., 2023; Johnson et al., 2016; Shemesh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Telomeric proteins, and in particular the CST, can be regulated by SUMO modification.
source: Previous studies found that telomeric proteins, and in particular the CST, can be regulated by SUMO modification (Hang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SUMOylation of PCNA plays a role in the regulation of telomere length.
source: Here we show that SUMOylation of PCNA plays a role in the regulation of telomere length and uncovers an interaction between the Elg1 RLC and the CST.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: PCNA SUMOylation positively regulates telomerase activity.
source: We report that PCNA SUMOylation positively regulates telomerase activity, and its unloading by the Elg1-RLC is essential for normal telomere size regulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Unloading of PCNA by the Elg1-RLC is essential for normal telomere size regulation.
source: We report that PCNA SUMOylation positively regulates telomerase activity, and its unloading by the Elg1-RLC is essential for normal telomere size regulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Stn1 during late S-phase.
source: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Stn1 during late S-phase and mediates the interaction between Stn1 and Cdc13 after PCNA has been unloaded from the telomeres.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The N-terminus of Elg1 mediates the interaction between Stn1 and Cdc13 after PCNA has been unloaded from the telomeres.
source: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Stn1 during late S-phase and mediates the interaction between Stn1 and Cdc13 after PCNA has been unloaded from the telomeres.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Mutations in POL30 at lysine 127 have little effect on telomere length by themselves.
source: Figure 1 shows that the mutations in POL30 have little effect by themselves.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mutations in POL30 at lysine 164 have little effect on telomere length by themselves.
source: Figure 1 shows that the mutations in POL30 have little effect by themselves.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Single mutations in POL30 at K127R or K164R did not affect the long telomeres of elg1Δ.
source: Importantly, whereas the single mutants did not affect the long telomeres of elg1Δ, mutating both lysine residues of each PCNA subunit completely abrogated the long telomere phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mutating both lysine residues K127 and K164 of PCNA completely abrogated the long telomere phenotype of elg1Δ.
source: Importantly, whereas the single mutants did not affect the long telomeres of elg1Δ, mutating both lysine residues of each PCNA subunit completely abrogated the long telomere phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Lysine 164 of PCNA can be modified by both SUMO and ubiquitin.
source: Lysine 164 can be modified by both SUMO and ubiquitin; mutating only this residue prevents ubiquitination, but not SUMOylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCNA modifications.

claim: Mutating lysine 164 of PCNA prevents ubiquitination, but not SUMOylation.
source: Lysine 164 can be modified by both SUMO and ubiquitin; mutating only this residue prevents ubiquitination, but not SUMOylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCNA modifications.

claim: The pol30-K164R mutant shows no effect on the long telomere phenotype of elg1Δ.
source: Figure 1 demonstrates that this mutant shows no effect.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RAD18 encodes the E3 ubiquitin ligase required to ubiquitinate PCNA.
source: To ensure that SUMO, and not ubiquitin, is the modification responsible for the long telomeres of elg1Δ, we deleted RAD18, encoding the E3 ubiquitin ligase required to ubiquitinate PCNA (Hoege et al., 2002; Stelter and Ulrich, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Lack of Rad18 has no effect on the elongated telomeres of elg1Δ.
source: Figure 1 shows that lack of Rad18 has no effect on the elongated telomeres of elg1Δ.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SUMOylation of PCNA is required for the long telomeres phenotype of elg1Δ mutants.
source: We conclude that SUMOylation of PCNA is required for the long telomeres phenotype of elg1Δ mutants.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Telomeres become elongated upon overexpression of wild-type PCNA.
source: Figure 1B shows that telomeres become elongated upon overexpression of the wild-type protein (which can be modified), or the Pol30-RR version fused to SUMO, but do not elongate upon overexpression of the unmodifiable Pol30-RR version, or the one fused to ubiquitin.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Telomeres become elongated upon overexpression of Pol30-RR fused to SUMO.
source: Figure 1B shows that telomeres become elongated upon overexpression of the wild-type protein (which can be modified), or the Pol30-RR version fused to SUMO, but do not elongate upon overexpression of the unmodifiable Pol30-RR version, or the one fused to ubiquitin.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Telomeres do not elongate upon overexpression of the unmodifiable Pol30-RR version.
source: Figure 1B shows that telomeres become elongated upon overexpression of the wild-type protein (which can be modified), or the Pol30-RR version fused to SUMO, but do not elongate upon overexpression of the unmodifiable Pol30-RR version, or the one fused to ubiquitin.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Telomeres do not elongate upon overexpression of Pol30-RR fused to ubiquitin.
source: Figure 1B shows that telomeres become elongated upon overexpression of the wild-type protein (which can be modified), or the Pol30-RR version fused to SUMO, but do not elongate upon overexpression of the unmodifiable Pol30-RR version, or the one fused to ubiquitin.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Accumulation of SUMOylated PCNA is both necessary and sufficient for telomere elongation in the presence or absence of Elg1.
source: These results, together with those of Figure 1A, show that accumulation of SUMOylated PCNA, and not unmodified or ubiquitinated PCNA, is both necessary and sufficient for telomere elongation in the presence or in the absence of Elg1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The elongated telomere phenotype of Elg1 was identified in systematic screens of the yeast knockout collection.
source: The elongated telomere phenotype of Elg1 was identified in systematic screens of the yeast knockout collection (Askree et al., 2004; Gatbonton et al., 2006), together with ~200 additional mutants of similar phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to systematic screens.

claim: Approximately 200 additional mutants with elongated telomere phenotypes were identified in systematic screens of the yeast knockout collection.
source: The elongated telomere phenotype of Elg1 was identified in systematic screens of the yeast knockout collection (Askree et al., 2004; Gatbonton et al., 2006), together with ~200 additional mutants of similar phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to systematic screens.

claim: Most double mutants of elg1Δ combined with other long telomere mutants exhibited telomeres longer than each of the single mutants.
source: Most double mutants exhibited telomeres longer than each of the single mutants, indicating that they affect different pathways.
evidence: This is based on systematic genetic analysis described in the text.

claim: The double mutant of elg1Δ and rrp8Δ showed epistasis (the double mutant was not longer than the single mutants).
source: One of the mutants showing clear epistasis (the double mutant was not longer than the single mutants) carried a deletion of RRP8, a gene involved in modification of the ribosomal RNA.
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis described in the text.

claim: RRP8 is a gene involved in modification of the ribosomal RNA.
source: One of the mutants showing clear epistasis (the double mutant was not longer than the single mutants) carried a deletion of RRP8, a gene involved in modification of the ribosomal RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RRP8 function.

claim: The deletion of RRP8 caused a decrease in the expression of its neighboring gene, STN1.
source: Further analysis demonstrated that the knockout of RRP8 exhibited the 'neighboring gene effect,' and in fact the deletion of RRP8 caused a decrease in the expression of its neighboring gene, STN1 (Ben-Shitrit et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on the neighboring gene effect.

claim: The telomeres of the elg1Δ stn1-13 double mutant are not longer than those of the single mutants.
source: The telomeres of the double mutants are not longer than those of the single mutants (Figure 2A), indicating that Elg1 works in the same TLM pathway as Stn1.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The telomeres of the elg1Δ stn1-164 double mutant are not longer than those of the single mutants.
source: The telomeres of the double mutants are not longer than those of the single mutants (Figure 2A), indicating that Elg1 works in the same TLM pathway as Stn1.
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Elg1 works in the same telomere length maintenance pathway as Stn1.
source: The telomeres of the double mutants are not longer than those of the single mutants (Figure 2A), indicating that Elg1 works in the same TLM pathway as Stn1.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of epitope-tagged Elg1 pulled down Stn1.
source: IP of epitope-tagged Elg1 pulled down Stn1 but not the other two members of the CST complex, Cdc13 or Ten1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of epitope-tagged Elg1 did not pull down Cdc13.
source: IP of epitope-tagged Elg1 pulled down Stn1 but not the other two members of the CST complex, Cdc13 or Ten1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of epitope-tagged Elg1 did not pull down Ten1.
source: IP of epitope-tagged Elg1 pulled down Stn1 but not the other two members of the CST complex, Cdc13 or Ten1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Elg1 protein can be divided into three main functional domains: an N-terminal domain (amino acids 1–234), a central AAA domain (amino acids 235–514), and a C-terminal domain (amino acids 515–791).
source: For our YTH experiments, the Elg1 protein was divided into three main functional domains: an N-terminal domain (amino acids 1–234), a central AAA domain (amino acids 235–514), and a C-terminal domain (amino acids 515–791) (Itzkovich et al., 2023; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis cited in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The AAA and C-terminal domains of Elg1 contain the conserved RFC boxes.
source: The AAA and C-terminal domains contain the conserved RFC boxes and are required for the interactions with the small RFC subunits, shared by all RFC-like domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Elg1 structure.

claim: The AAA and C-terminal domains of Elg1 are required for the interactions with the small RFC subunits.
source: The AAA and C-terminal domains contain the conserved RFC boxes and are required for the interactions with the small RFC subunits, shared by all RFC-like domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Elg1 structure.

claim: The N-terminal domain of Elg1 is unique to Elg1.
source: The N-terminal domain (hereafter referred to as NTD) is unique to Elg1 (Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacted strongly with Cdc13 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacted strongly with Cdc13 and Stn1, and weakly with Ten1 (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacted strongly with Stn1 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacted strongly with Cdc13 and Stn1, and weakly with Ten1 (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacted weakly with Ten1 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacted strongly with Cdc13 and Stn1, and weakly with Ten1 (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No interaction was detected between Elg1's CTD and Cdc13, Stn1, or Ten1 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: In contrast, no interaction was detected with Elg1's CTD.
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Cdc13 interacts with SUMO in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: We could also detect interactions of Cdc13, Stn1, and Elg1's NTD with SUMO (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Stn1 interacts with SUMO in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: We could also detect interactions of Cdc13, Stn1, and Elg1's NTD with SUMO (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Elg1's NTD interacts with SUMO in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: We could also detect interactions of Cdc13, Stn1, and Elg1's NTD with SUMO (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The NTD of Elg1 contains SUMO-interacting motifs (SIMs).
source: The NTD contains SUMO-interacting motifs (SIMs), which were previously shown to interact with SUMO and the SUMO machinery (Parnas et al., 2011; Parnas et al., 2010; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The SIMs in Elg1's NTD were previously shown to interact with SUMO and the SUMO machinery.
source: The NTD contains SUMO-interacting motifs (SIMs), which were previously shown to interact with SUMO and the SUMO machinery (Parnas et al., 2011; Parnas et al., 2010; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The interaction of Elg1's NTD with Stn1 was abolished when the SIM motifs were mutated.
source: Interestingly, the interaction of Elg1's NTD with Stn1, but not with Cdc13, was abolished when the SIM motifs (amino acids I27A, I93K, I121A, and I122A) were mutated (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The interaction of Elg1's NTD with Cdc13 was not abolished when the SIM motifs were mutated.
source: Interestingly, the interaction of Elg1's NTD with Stn1, but not with Cdc13, was abolished when the SIM motifs (amino acids I27A, I93K, I121A, and I122A) were mutated (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed reduced physical interaction between Elg1-sim and Stn1.
source: We confirmed these results by co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The interaction with Stn1 is mediated by SUMOylation of a protein.
source: These results suggest that the interaction with Stn1 is mediated by SUMOylation of a protein, whereas the interaction of Cdc13 with Elg1-NTD is independent of the SIM in the plasmid-borne copy of Elg1.
evidence: This is inferred from the YTH and co-IP data.

claim: The interaction of Cdc13 with Elg1-NTD is independent of the SIM in the plasmid-borne copy of Elg1.
source: These results suggest that the interaction with Stn1 is mediated by SUMOylation of a protein, whereas the interaction of Cdc13 with Elg1-NTD is independent of the SIM in the plasmid-borne copy of Elg1.
evidence: This is inferred from the YTH data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Deletion of SIZ1 and SIZ2 abolishes the interaction of Stn1 and Cdc13 with Elg1's NTD.
source: Figure 3D shows that indeed deletion of the genes encoding these enzymes abolishes the interaction of Stn1 and Cdc13 with Elg1's NTD.
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SUMO plays a role in mediating the Elg1-CST interactions.
source: We conclude that SUMO plays a role in mediating the Elg1-CST interactions.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the YTH data in various genetic backgrounds.

claim: Elg1 preferentially interacts with SUMOylated PCNA.
source: Since Elg1 preferentially interacts with SUMOylated PCNA (Parnas et al., 2010) and Stn1 can bind SUMO noncovalently in YTH (Figure 3C), we reckoned that SUMOylated PCNA may mediate the interaction between Stn1 and Elg1.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Stn1 can bind SUMO noncovalently in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: Since Elg1 preferentially interacts with SUMOylated PCNA (Parnas et al., 2010) and Stn1 can bind SUMO noncovalently in YTH (Figure 3C), we reckoned that SUMOylated PCNA may mediate the interaction between Stn1 and Elg1.
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Elg1 and Stn1 can still interact in the pol30-RR strain.
source: We found, however, that Elg1 and Stn1 could still interact in the pol30-RR strain (Figure 3D), despite the fact that PCNA cannot become SUMOylated.
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A different SUMOylated target (not PCNA) mediates the interaction between Elg1 and Stn1.
source: Consequently, a different SUMOylated target seems to mediate the interaction between Elg1 and Stn1, or else either one of the proteins is SUMOylated.
evidence: This is inferred from the YTH data in pol30-RR background.

claim: Deletion of SIZ1 and SIZ2 completely abolished the interactions between Elg1's NTD and Cdc13.
source: We also noted that, despite the fact that mutation in the plasmid-borne NTD's SIM had no effect on the interaction with Cdc13 (Figure 3B), deletion of SIZ1 and SIZ2, and mutation in the SUMOylation sites in PCNA completely abolished the interactions between Elg1's NTD and Cdc13 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutation in the SUMOylation sites in PCNA completely abolished the interactions between Elg1's NTD and Cdc13.
source: We also noted that, despite the fact that mutation in the plasmid-borne NTD's SIM had no effect on the interaction with Cdc13 (Figure 3B), deletion of SIZ1 and SIZ2, and mutation in the SUMOylation sites in PCNA completely abolished the interactions between Elg1's NTD and Cdc13 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PCNA SUMOylation is necessary for the interaction between Elg1 and Cdc13.
source: This implies that PCNA SUMOylation is necessary for the interaction between Elg1 and Cdc13.
evidence: This is inferred from the YTH data in various genetic backgrounds.

claim: Cdc13 physically interacts with PCNA.
source: We confirmed by co-IP that Cdc13 indeed physically interacts with PCNA (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The interaction between Cdc13 and PCNA was almost completely abolished when PCNA could not be SUMOylated.
source: The interaction between Cdc13 and PCNA was almost completely abolished when PCNA could not be SUMOylated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The interaction between Cdc13 and both PCNA and Elg1 is dependent on SUMOylation of PCNA.
source: In summary, the interaction between Cdc13 and both PCNA and Elg1, but not that of Elg1 with Stn1, is dependent on SUMOylation of PCNA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the YTH and co-IP data.

claim: The interaction between Elg1 and Stn1 is not dependent on SUMOylation of PCNA.
source: In summary, the interaction between Cdc13 and both PCNA and Elg1, but not that of Elg1 with Stn1, is dependent on SUMOylation of PCNA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the YTH data.

claim: Cdc13 failed to interact with the plasmid-borne Elg1-NTD in a strain in which the ELG1 gene is deleted from the genome.
source: When we repeated the YTH assays in a strain in which the ELG1 gene is deleted from the genome, we were surprised to see that now Cdc13 failed to interact with the plasmid-borne Elg1-NTD (Figure 4A, compare to Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The interaction between Stn1 and Elg1-NTD was not affected by the deletion of the genomic ELG1.
source: In contrast, the interaction between Stn1 and Elg1-NTD was not affected by the deletion of the genomic ELG1.
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Stn1 interacts directly with the plasmid-borne Elg1-NTD, via its SIM-mediated SUMO-binding.
source: Taken together, these results imply that whereas Stn1 interacts directly with the plasmid-borne Elg1-NTD, via its SIM-mediated SUMO-binding, the interaction with Cdc13 require both PCNA SUMOylation and the genomic ELG1 gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the YTH data in various genetic backgrounds.

claim: The interaction with Cdc13 requires both PCNA SUMOylation and the genomic ELG1 gene.
source: Taken together, these results imply that whereas Stn1 interacts directly with the plasmid-borne Elg1-NTD, via its SIM-mediated SUMO-binding, the interaction with Cdc13 require both PCNA SUMOylation and the genomic ELG1 gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the YTH data in various genetic backgrounds.

claim: In strains carrying genomic elg1-DD and elg1-sim+DD alleles, Cdc13 failed to interact with plasmid borne Elg1-NTD.
source: We found that in strains carrying genomic elg1-DD and elg1-sim+DD alleles, Cdc13 failed to interact with plasmid borne Elg1-NTD, whereas in the elg1-sim strain the interaction was weak but clearly seen (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: In the elg1-sim strain, the interaction between Cdc13 and plasmid borne Elg1-NTD was weak but clearly seen.
source: We found that in strains carrying genomic elg1-DD and elg1-sim+DD alleles, Cdc13 failed to interact with plasmid borne Elg1-NTD, whereas in the elg1-sim strain the interaction was weak but clearly seen (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The PCNA unloading activity of Elg1 is essential to allow the interaction between Cdc13 and the plasmid borne Elg1-NTD.
source: This observation indicates that the PCNA unloading activity of Elg1 is essential to allow the interaction between Cdc13 and the plasmid borne Elg1-NTD: this activity is high in elg1-sim mutants, intermediate in the elg1-DD strain, and is abolished by the elg1-sim+DD mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the YTH data with different elg1 alleles.

claim: PCNA unloading activity is high in elg1-sim mutants.
source: This observation indicates that the PCNA unloading activity of Elg1 is essential to allow the interaction between Cdc13 and the plasmid borne Elg1-NTD: this activity is high in elg1-sim mutants, intermediate in the elg1-DD strain, and is abolished by the elg1-sim+DD mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these alleles, cited in the manuscript.

claim: PCNA unloading activity is intermediate in the elg1-DD strain.
source: This observation indicates that the PCNA unloading activity of Elg1 is essential to allow the interaction between Cdc13 and the plasmid borne Elg1-NTD: this activity is high in elg1-sim mutants, intermediate in the elg1-DD strain, and is abolished by the elg1-sim+DD mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these alleles, cited in the manuscript.

claim: PCNA unloading activity is abolished by the elg1-sim+DD mutations.
source: This observation indicates that the PCNA unloading activity of Elg1 is essential to allow the interaction between Cdc13 and the plasmid borne Elg1-NTD: this activity is high in elg1-sim mutants, intermediate in the elg1-DD strain, and is abolished by the elg1-sim+DD mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these alleles, cited in the manuscript.

claim: No interaction between the plasmid-borne Elg1 NTD and Cdc13 could be detected in the elg1-WalkerA mutant.
source: Figure 4E shows that no interaction between the plasmid-borne Elg1 NTD and Cdc13 could be detected despite the fact that functional SIMs are present both at the NTD and in the genome-encoded Elg1-WalkerA protein.
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The elg1-WalkerA mutant lacks ATPase and PCNA unloading activity.
source: We confirmed this idea by analyzing the interaction between Cdc13 and Elg1's NTD in another SIM-containing mutant strain devoid of PCNA unloading activity, elg1-WalkerA (KK343/4DD), which lacks ATPase and PCNA unloading activity (Itzkovich et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge about this allele, cited in the manuscript.

claim: The interaction with Stn1 is direct and mediated by the SUMOylation of a protein (different from PCNA).
source: We conclude that whereas the interaction with Stn1 is direct and mediated by the SUMOylation of a protein (different from PCNA), the interaction between Elg1's NTD and Cdc13 is indirect and can only take place after PCNA has been SUMOylated and unloaded.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the YTH data in various genetic backgrounds.

claim: The interaction between Elg1's NTD and Cdc13 is indirect and can only take place after PCNA has been SUMOylated and unloaded.
source: We conclude that whereas the interaction with Stn1 is direct and mediated by the SUMOylation of a protein (different from PCNA), the interaction between Elg1's NTD and Cdc13 is indirect and can only take place after PCNA has been SUMOylated and unloaded.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the YTH data in various genetic backgrounds.

claim: The presence of SUMOylated PCNA at telomeres may serve as a positive signal for telomerase activity.
source: This suggests a model for the coordination of telomerase activity and DNA replication: the presence of SUMOylated PCNA at telomeres may serve as a positive signal for telomerase activity.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Once Elg1 unloads PCNA, Stn1-Elg1 can bind Cdc13, ending telomerase activity.
source: Once Elg1 unloads PCNA, however, Stn1-Elg1 can bind Cdc13, ending telomerase activity.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Cdc13 undergoes SUMOylation.
source: Cdc13 undergoes SUMOylation, and this modification plays an essential role in the negative regulation of telomere length (Hang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SUMOylation of Cdc13 plays an essential role in the negative regulation of telomere length.
source: Cdc13 undergoes SUMOylation, and this modification plays an essential role in the negative regulation of telomere length (Hang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutations of the Cdc13 SUMOylation sites (cdc13-snm) weaken its interaction with Stn1.
source: Accordingly, mutations of the Cdc13 SUMOylation sites (cdc13-snm, 'SUMO no more') weaken its interaction with Stn1 and lead to elongated telomere phenotype (Hang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutations of the Cdc13 SUMOylation sites (cdc13-snm) lead to elongated telomere phenotype.
source: Accordingly, mutations of the Cdc13 SUMOylation sites (cdc13-snm, 'SUMO no more') weaken its interaction with Stn1 and lead to elongated telomere phenotype (Hang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Preventing SUMOylation of Cdc13 abolishes the interaction between this protein and Elg1.
source: Figure 4F shows that indeed preventing SUMOylation of Cdc13 abolishes the interaction between this protein and Elg1.
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SUMOylation of the plasmid-borne version of Cdc13 (i.e., in cis) is required for interactions with Elg1 in the YTH assay.
source: Thus, SUMOylation of the plasmid-borne version of Cdc13 (i.e., in cis) is required for these interactions in the YTH assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the YTH data with cdc13-snm.

claim: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Cdc13 only if Cdc13 can be SUMOylated.
source: In summary, the N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Cdc13 only if (1) Cdc13 can be SUMOylated (Figure 4F), (2) PCNA can be SUMOylated (Figure 3D), and (3) PCNA can be unloaded (Figure 4A, C–E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the YTH data.

claim: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Cdc13 only if PCNA can be SUMOylated.
source: In summary, the N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Cdc13 only if (1) Cdc13 can be SUMOylated (Figure 4F), (2) PCNA can be SUMOylated (Figure 3D), and (3) PCNA can be unloaded (Figure 4A, C–E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the YTH data.

claim: The N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Cdc13 only if PCNA can be unloaded.
source: In summary, the N-terminus of Elg1 interacts with Cdc13 only if (1) Cdc13 can be SUMOylated (Figure 4F), (2) PCNA can be SUMOylated (Figure 3D), and (3) PCNA can be unloaded (Figure 4A, C–E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the YTH data.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Stn1 has been shown to be the region that interacts with Cdc13.
source: To further dissect this point, we divided the Stn1 protein into an NTD (first 281 amino acids) and a CTD (amino acids 282–495). The later has been shown to be the region that interacts with Cdc13 (Petreaca et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The NTD of Elg1 interacts with Stn1 via its C-terminal domain, both in WT and elg1∆ strains.
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 2B shows that the NTD of Elg1 also interacts with Stn1 via its C-terminal domain, both in WT and elg1∆ strains.
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Pol3 was co-IPed with Elg1 strongly only during the S-phase.
source: Pol3 was co-IPed with Elg1 strongly only during the S-phase (40–70 min, 120–140 min), whereas Stn1 was only detected in late S-phase (60–70 min, 140–160 min) for both cell cycles and was barely detected in G1 (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Stn1 was only detected in late S-phase (60–70 min, 140–160 min) for both cell cycles and was barely detected in G1.
source: Pol3 was co-IPed with Elg1 strongly only during the S-phase (40–70 min, 120–140 min), whereas Stn1 was only detected in late S-phase (60–70 min, 140–160 min) for both cell cycles and was barely detected in G1 (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The timing of Elg1-Stn1 interaction coincides with telomerase activity at telomeres, which is low in early to mid S-phase and peaks in late S-phase.
source: This pattern coincides with telomerase activity at telomeres, which is low in early to mid S-phase and peaks in late S-phase (Puglisi et al., 2008; Taggart et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The timing of arrival of PCNA to the telomeres (60–70 min into the cell cycle) coincides with the timing of the co-IP between Elg1 and Stn1.
source: Figure 5D shows that the timing of arrival of PCNA to the telomeres (60–70 min into the cell cycle) coincides with the timing of the co-IP between Elg1 and Stn1 (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the Telo-ChIP data shown in Figure 5D and co-IP data in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Elg1 moves with the replication fork, and interacts with Stn1 at the end of S-phase, when telomeres are replicated and telomerase is activated.
source: Thus, our results are consistent with the idea that Elg1 moves with the replication fork, and interacts with Stn1 at the end of S-phase, when telomeres are replicated and telomerase is activated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-IP and ChIP data.

claim: Both Elg1 and Cdc13 bind Stn1 at its C-terminus.
source: Since both Elg1 and Cdc13 bind Stn1 at its C-terminus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Petreaca et al., 2007), it is possible that the absence of Elg1 may affect the interaction between the two CST members.
evidence: This is based on YTH data and cited literature.

claim: When Elg1 was absent, Stn1 exhibited a strong reduction in its co-precipitation with Cdc13.
source: When Elg1 was absent, Stn1 exhibited a strong reduction in its co-precipitation with Cdc13 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The interaction between Stn1 and Cdc13 is, at least partly, dependent on Elg1.
source: This suggests that the interaction between Stn1 and Cdc13 is, at least partly, dependent on Elg1.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing reduced interaction in elg1Δ.

claim: Following firing of the origin proximal to the telomeres at late S-phase, Elg1 moves with the fork, unloading PCNA from the lagging strand as the fork progresses.
source: Following firing of the origin proximal to the telomeres at late S-phase, Elg1 moves with the fork, unloading PCNA from the lagging strand as the fork progresses (Kubota et al., 2015; Kubota et al., 2013; Shemesh et al., 2017; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by cited literature and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SUMOylation of PCNA acts as a signal for the activation of telomerase.
source: SUMOylation of PCNA acts as a signal for the activation of telomerase (Figures 1A, B, 6B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Once Elg1 reaches the telomeres, it interacts with Stn1.
source: Once Elg1 reaches the telomeres, it interacts with Stn1 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The Elg1-Stn1 interaction requires SUMOylation of Stn1 or of some other protein, which is not PCNA nor Cdc13.
source: This interaction requires SUMOylation of Stn1 or of some other protein, which is not PCNA (Figure 3D) nor Cdc13 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and could be Stn1 itself or another telomeric protein (Hang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, based on YTH data and cited literature.

claim: The Elg1-Stn1 complex unloads the SUMOylated PCNA at the telomeres.
source: The Elg1-Stn1 complex then unloads the SUMOylated PCNA at the telomeres, and Cdc13 becomes SUMOylated (Figure 6C), now interacting with Elg1-Stn1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cdc13 becomes SUMOylated after the Elg1-Stn1 complex unloads SUMOylated PCNA at the telomeres.
source: The Elg1-Stn1 complex then unloads the SUMOylated PCNA at the telomeres, and Cdc13 becomes SUMOylated (Figure 6C), now interacting with Elg1-Stn1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SUMOylation of Cdc13 allows its interaction with Stn1, and presumably with Ten1, creating the complete CST complex, and preventing further telomerase activity.
source: SUMOylation of Cdc13 allows its interaction with Stn1, and presumably with Ten1 (Hang et al., 2011), creating the complete CST complex, and preventing further telomerase activity (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by cited literature and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Co-IP experiments detect a strong interaction with Stn1 but fail to detect an interaction with Cdc13.
source: The fact that co-IP experiments detect a strong interaction with Stn1 but fail to detect an interaction with Cdc13 (Figure 2B) suggests that indeed the interaction Elg1-Cdc13 is very transient, and Elg1 leaves chromatin immediately, leaving the C-terminus of Stn1 free to interact with Cdc13.
evidence: This is based on the co-IP data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The interaction Elg1-Cdc13 is very transient, and Elg1 leaves chromatin immediately, leaving the C-terminus of Stn1 free to interact with Cdc13.
source: The fact that co-IP experiments detect a strong interaction with Stn1 but fail to detect an interaction with Cdc13 (Figure 2B) suggests that indeed the interaction Elg1-Cdc13 is very transient, and Elg1 leaves chromatin immediately, leaving the C-terminus of Stn1 free to interact with Cdc13.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data.

claim: Two negative regulators of telomerase activity, Elg1 and Stn1, work in the same pathway to coordinate chromosomal DNA replication and telomere elongation.
source: We have presented evidence for the fact that two negative regulators of telomerase activity, Elg1 and Stn1, work in the same pathway to coordinate chromosomal DNA replication and telomere elongation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The unloading of SUMOylated PCNA by Elg1 at telomeres facilitates the interaction between Stn1 and Cdc13 that negatively regulate telomerase activity.
source: We present a model (Figure 6) in which the unloading of SUMOylated PCNA by Elg1 at telomeres facilitates the interaction between Stn1 and Cdc13 that negatively regulate telomerase activity.
evidence: This is the main model proposed in the study, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The double mutants of Elg1 and Stn1 do not show increased telomere length phenotype in comparison to the single mutants.
source: First, the double mutants of Elg1 and Stn1 do not show increased telomere length phenotype in comparison to the single mutants, indicating that both proteins work in the same pathway that negatively regulates telomere length (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The interaction between Elg1 and Stn1 seems direct and occurs exclusively during the late S-phase.
source: In addition, the interaction between Elg1 and Stn1 seems direct and occurs exclusively during the late S-phase (Figures 2B and 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figures 2B and 5A-C.

claim: The interaction between Elg1 and Stn1 is neither dependent on SUMOylation of PCNA nor on Cdc13.
source: This interaction is neither dependent on SUMOylation of PCNA (Figure 3D) nor on Cdc13 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The interaction between Cdc13 and Elg1 is dependent on both the SUMOylation of PCNA and of Cdc13 itself.
source: In contrast, the interaction between Cdc13 and Elg1 is dependent on both the SUMOylation of PCNA (Figure 3D) and of Cdc13 itself (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by the YTH data shown in Figures 3D and 4F.

claim: Elg1 participates in the negative regulation of telomere length by unloading SUMOylated PCNA from the telomeres.
source: We suggest that Elg1 participates in the negative regulation of telomere length by unloading SUMOylated PCNA from the telomeres.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Unloading of SUMOylated PCNA eliminates a positive signal for telomerase activity.
source: This eliminates a positive signal for telomerase activity and causes the exchange of Est1 by Stn1 as interactor of Cdc13, effectively terminating telomerase activity (Chandra et al., 2001; Gao et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2020; Hang et al., 2011; Puglisi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by cited literature.

claim: Unloading of SUMOylated PCNA causes the exchange of Est1 by Stn1 as interactor of Cdc13, effectively terminating telomerase activity.
source: This eliminates a positive signal for telomerase activity and causes the exchange of Est1 by Stn1 as interactor of Cdc13, effectively terminating telomerase activity (Chandra et al., 2001; Gao et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2020; Hang et al., 2011; Puglisi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model, supported by cited literature.

claim: ELG1 is the only PCNA unloader in eukaryotes.
source: ELG1 is the only PCNA unloader in eukaryotes; however, it is not an essential gene, implying that there are alternative ways in which PCNA can get unloaded (either spontaneously or with the help of RFC) (Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ELG1 is not an essential gene.
source: ELG1 is the only PCNA unloader in eukaryotes; however, it is not an essential gene, implying that there are alternative ways in which PCNA can get unloaded (either spontaneously or with the help of RFC) (Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: There are alternative ways in which PCNA can get unloaded (either spontaneously or with the help of RFC).
source: ELG1 is the only PCNA unloader in eukaryotes; however, it is not an essential gene, implying that there are alternative ways in which PCNA can get unloaded (either spontaneously or with the help of RFC) (Arbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that ELG1 is not essential, supported by citation.

claim: pol30-RR mutants have stable, normal-sized telomeres.
source: The fact that pol30-RR mutants have stable, normal-sized telomeres (Figure 1) implies that despite lacking PCNA SUMOylation, they are able to solve the 'end replication problem.'
evidence: This is supported by the teloblot data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Despite lacking PCNA SUMOylation, pol30-RR mutants are able to solve the 'end replication problem.'
source: The fact that pol30-RR mutants have stable, normal-sized telomeres (Figure 1) implies that despite lacking PCNA SUMOylation, they are able to solve the 'end replication problem.'
evidence: This is inferred from the teloblot data.

claim: There are two alternative modes of telomerase: one carrying 'basal activity,' with minimal genetic requirements, able to maintain most telomeres at normal size, and another, 'sustained activity,' required for increased elongating activity.
source: Our results support the notion (Maicher et al., 2017) that there are two alternative modes of telomerase: one carrying 'basal activity,' with minimal genetic requirements, able to maintain most telomeres at normal size, and another, 'sustained activity,' required for increased elongating activity (Maicher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The first mode of telomerase does not require Rnr1, the large subunit of the ribonucleotide reductase enzyme, whereas the second depends on it.
source: Previous results have shown that the first mode does not require Rnr1, the large subunit of the ribonucleotide reductase enzyme, whereas the second depends on it (Maicher et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SUMOylated PCNA is only needed for the second mode of telomerase (sustained activity).
source: Similarly, SUMOylated PCNA is only needed for the second mode of telomerase.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and comparison to the two-mode model.

claim: SUMOylation often works by targeting many physically interacting proteins together.
source: It has been proposed that SUMOylation often works by targeting many physically interacting proteins together. This may be executed by the local recruitment of SUMO ligases to preassembled, co-localized protein groups. SUMOylation thus may increase their interactions, acting to increase their local concentration or effective interaction (Jentsch and Psakhye, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SUMOylation of telomeric proteins seems to be a case where SUMOylation targets many physically interacting proteins together.
source: SUMOylation of telomeric proteins seems to be one of those cases (Garg et al., 2014; Hang et al., 2011; Matmati et al., 2018; Miyagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on SUMOylation of telomeric proteins.

claim: PCNA, Cdc13, and possibly Stn1 undergo SUMOylation to ensure the proper sequence of events in the coordination between telomerase activity and chromosomal replication.
source: In our model, PCNA, Cdc13, and possibly Stn1 undergo SUMOylation to ensure the proper sequence of events in the coordination between telomerase activity and chromosomal replication.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Cdc13 binds Pol12, a subunit of Polymerase Alpha.
source: Cdc13 binds Pol12, a subunit of Polymerase Alpha (Grossi et al., 2004; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008), allowing the synthesis of the lagging strand on the newly synthesized ssDNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cdc13 binding to Pol12 allows the synthesis of the lagging strand on the newly synthesized ssDNA.
source: Cdc13 binds Pol12, a subunit of Polymerase Alpha (Grossi et al., 2004; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008), allowing the synthesis of the lagging strand on the newly synthesized ssDNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The arrival of the replisome to a short telomere at the end of S-phase brings PCNA, whose SUMOylation can elicit both telomerase activity, and its subsequent repression when PCNA is unloaded by Elg1.
source: Thus, the arrival of the replisome to a short telomere at the end of S-phase brings PCNA, whose SUMOylation can elicit both telomerase activity, and its subsequent repression when PCNA is unloaded by Elg1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: PCNA unloading by Elg1 primes synthesis of the complementary strand, thus coordinating telomere elongation with chromosomal replication.
source: This in turn primes synthesis of the complementary strand, thus coordinating telomere elongation with chromosomal replication.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.
